Empirical Research Plan  
“Does greater treatment intensity for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) among the elderly reduce mortality?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–Stage Least Squares (2SLS) Instrumental‐Variables design.

Instrument(s)  
A. Differential-distance (DD) instrument  
   DDᵢ = (distance from patient i’s ZIP centroid to the nearest “high-intensity” hospital)  
        – (distance to the nearest “low-intensity” hospital)

B. (Robustness) Hospital-style instrument  
   STYLE_h,t-1 = average AMI treatment intensity delivered by hospital h to all AMI patients in the previous calendar year (exclude current-year patients).

Why IV?  
• Treatment intensity is chosen by physicians and may be correlated with unobserved patient severity ⇒ OLS biased.  
• Where an ambulance brings a patient (or which close hospital the patient self-presents to) is driven largely by geography and EMS routing protocols, which are plausibly unrelated to unobserved health.  
• DD or lagged style is strongly predictive of received intensity (relevance) yet should affect 30-day / 1-year mortality only through the intensity of treatment, conditional on rich covariates (exclusion).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
INTENSITYᵢ: continuous index = standardized sum of invasive AMI procedures within 7 days of admission  
• coronary catheterization  
• PCI / angioplasty  
• CABG surgery  
(scale to mean 0, SD 1)  
We will later also dichotomise: HIGH_INTᵢ = 1[INTENSITYᵢ ≥ 75th pct].

Control group  
Patients with lower intensity (or the continuous counterfactual).

Key variation  
Cross-sectional (and over-time) differences in hospital practice style captured through DD or STYLE instruments.

Timing  
Treatment occurs at admission (day 0–7). Outcomes: 30-day and 1-year mortality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
IV1. Relevance Cov(Z, INTENSITY) ≠ 0  
   Highly plausible: DD and STYLE have been shown to explain large portions of treatment variation.

IV2. Exclusion Z affects mortality only via INTENSITY, not via other channels.  
   Plausible because: (i) conditional on demographics & pre-hospital comorbidities, residential distance mainly determines hospital choice, not underlying health; (ii) lagged STYLE uses last-year patients, so uncorrelated with current patient shocks. Still, hospital quality could be a channel (see threats).

IV3. Independence / Ignorability Z ⫫ ε | X  
   We condition on rich Medicare risk adjusters (Elixhauser comorbidities, prior spending, ZIP-code income, age-by-sex fixed effects) to bolster plausibility.

IV4. Monotonicity Higher DD cannot make any patient more likely to receive higher intensity (or vice-versa). Reasonable given shortest-distance EMS routing.

IV5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) One patient’s treatment does not affect another’s mortality. Reasonable at individual level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Selective sorting / bypass  
   Wealthier or more health-conscious patients may travel farther to high-tech hospitals.  
   • Use DD rather than simple distance; include ZIP-code–level socioeconomic controls; restrict to emergency ambulance arrivals; drop inter-hospital transfers.  
   • Conduct McCrary test on the distribution of DD to detect bunching.

2. Hospital quality correlated with intensity  
   High-intensity hospitals might also have better nursing ratios, PCI teams, etc.  
   • Include hospital fixed effects when using STYLE instrument (within-hospital over-time variation).  
   • Control for current-year hospital AMI volume, teaching status, and risk-adjusted mortality for non-cardiac admissions.  
   • Placebo: run IV on diseases where cath-lab intensity should not matter (e.g., hip fracture).

3. Measurement error in intensity index  
   Could attenuate first stage.  
   • Use procedure codes from both Part A & B claims; winsorise extreme values; replicate using total AMI episode spending.  
   • Report first-stage F-statistics; weak-instrument robust Anderson–Rubin CI if F < 10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#----------------------------------------------------
# 0) Packages
#----------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast iv regression
library(ivreg)        # alternative
library(modelsummary) # neat tables
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

#----------------------------------------------------
# 1) Load Medicare AMI data
#   Assume a patient-level file: "ami_medicare.csv"
#----------------------------------------------------
ami <- read_csv("ami_medicare.csv")

#----------------------------------------------------
# 2) Variable construction
#----------------------------------------------------
ami <- ami %>%
  mutate(
    # Intensity index (std)
    intensity_raw = cath + pci + cabg,               # numeric counts
    INTENSITY     = scale(intensity_raw)[,1],
    HIGH_INT      = as.integer(INTENSITY >= quantile(INTENSITY, .75, na.rm=TRUE)),
    
    # Outcomes
    mort30  = as.integer(death_within_30days == 1),
    mort365 = as.integer(death_within_365days == 1),
    
    # Instruments
    DD      = dist_high_int_hosp - dist_low_int_hosp,
    STYLE   = lag_hosp_intensity,                    # previous-year mean
    
    # Covariates
    age_cat = cut(age, breaks=c(65,70,75,80,85,90,120)),
    female  = as.integer(sex=="F")
  )

#----------------------------------------------------
# 3) Main IV specification
#    Outcome: 30-day mortality
#----------------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(
  mort30 ~ 1 | INTENSITY ~ DD | age_cat + female + race + 
            elixhauser_comorbs + zip_income_qtile, 
  data = ami, 
  cluster = ~hospital_id
)
etable(iv_main, se = "cluster")

#----------------------------------------------------
# 4) Robustness: within-hospital over-time (STYLE instrument)
#----------------------------------------------------
iv_style <- feols(
  mort30 ~ 1 | INTENSITY ~ STYLE | age_cat + female + race +
            elixhauser_comorbs + zip_income_qtile + hospital_id, 
  data = ami %>% filter(year %in% 2010:2018),
  cluster = ~hospital_id
)
etable(list(DD = iv_main, Style = iv_style), se = "cluster")

#----------------------------------------------------
# 5) Falsification test: Outcome = 30-day mortality after hip fracture
#----------------------------------------------------
hip <- read_csv("hipfx_medicare.csv")  # similar construction
hip <- hip %>% mutate(INTENSITY = scale(intensity_raw)[,1])
iv_placebo <- feols(
  mort30 ~ 1 | INTENSITY ~ DD | age_cat + female + race + elixhauser_comorbs,
  data = hip,
  cluster = ~hospital_id
)
etable(iv_placebo, se = "cluster")
```
Notes: `feols(y ~ 1 | endog ~ instr | controls)` uses fixest’s IV syntax. Replace covariate lists with actual variable names.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Medical intuition and prior literature suggest that timely invasive therapy (PCI, CABG) saves lives for suitable AMI patients. I expect:

• IV estimate on INTENSITY ≈ –0.02 to –0.04 for 30-day mortality  
  (i.e., a one-SD increase in intensity lowers 30-day mortality by about 2–4 percentage points from a baseline ≈18%).  
• Effects should attenuate but remain negative for 1-year mortality (~1–2 pp).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Relevance (first-stage F > 10) .................... 1  
2. Exclusion restriction believable .................. 0.7  
3. No endogenous sorting on instrument ............... 0.8  
4. Accurate measurement of treatment & outcome ....... 0.8  
5. Stable sample / no interference (SUTVA) ........... 1  

Total (out of 5) ..................................... 4.3

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan exploits plausibly exogenous geographic and practice-style variation to isolate the causal effect of AMI treatment intensity on elderly mortality, with transparent assumptions, robustness checks, and executable code.
